name: Secrets Coverage Gap Guard
description: Supplements the embedded gitleaks ruleset (agent/internal/policy/rules/gitleaks.toml, 195 rules) with specific named secret types from the competitor parity research's 222-rule Secrets catalog that gitleaks does not cover. Diffing all 222 names against the actual 195 gitleaks rule IDs found ~25 real gaps; this pack confidently encodes the 9 with a publicly documented, distinctive-enough format to write a safe regex for (most notably Anthropic API keys — a real gap for a product that is itself an AI-agent governance tool). The remaining ~16 gaps (Amazon Bedrock, Cisco Meraki, Heroku API Key v2, Artifactory API Key/Reference Token, ClickHouse Cloud API Key, Looker Client ID/Secret, Maxmind License Key, Freemius Secret Key, SettleMint's 3 token types, Sentry Org/User Token) are deliberately NOT included — each either has no publicly documented distinguishing format, or a format so generic (e.g. a bare 40-hex-char string, or a bare UUID) that a regex would be indistinguishable from countless non-secret strings. See docs/speakeasy-parity-gap-analysis.md for the full per-item reasoning.

rules.name: Require access request when gap-coverage secret patterns are detected in prompts or tool inputs
rules.description: Scans user prompts and tool call inputs for Anthropic (Admin and standard) API keys, Perplexity API keys, Notion integration tokens (legacy secret_ and current ntn_ formats), Airtable Personal Access Tokens, 1Password Secret Keys, and Sourcegraph and Sonar access tokens. Requires admin approval before these proceed into AI context.

rules.name: Redact gap-coverage secret patterns found in tool output
rules.description: Same pattern set as the prompt/input rule above, applied to tool output after execution. Redacts matches and allows execution to proceed with the sanitised data — does not block.

rules.name: Require access request to read PKCS #12 credential files
rules.description: PKCS #12 files (.p12/.pfx) bundle a private key and certificate chain, typically password-protected but still sensitive at rest. This is a file-extension check, not a content pattern — the competitor's "PKCS #12 File" rule is presumably the same kind of check on their side.
